lesson.menu_desc: The call that fails, and the polite repair that keeps you in it -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Say That Again
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 3 -- Say That Again

listenings.text: Right, I think we have everybody, so let me run through the agenda before we start. There are four items and I would like to be off this call in forty minutes, which means we will not solve the third one today, we will only scope it. Two quick things about how this works, because we have people joining from four time zones. First, if the line breaks up, say so immediately. Do not sit there hoping it improves, because it never does and we lose ten minutes reconstructing what you missed. Second, if you want to come in, just say the word, and I will bring you in. I would rather have three people talking over each other than one person going quiet for an hour and then sending an email that reopens everything. Right. Item one.

The single most useful thing I learned in twenty years of calls in a second language is that asking somebody to repeat is free. It costs you nothing. The person on the other end has no idea whether you missed it because of your English or because their microphone is terrible, and nine times out of ten it is their microphone. What is expensive is the other thing, which is nodding. You nod, the call ends, and now you are the one who has to reconstruct what was agreed from context, usually at eleven at night. I have a rule now. If I have not understood something twice, I stop the call and I ask, and I ask in a way that puts the problem on the line and not on the person: sorry, you are breaking up a bit, could you say that last part again. Nobody has ever been annoyed. Not once.
